A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SING by the same authors. The main text, appendices A–L, equations, and experimental displays support reliable comparison despite reformatting and added studies.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix L report original synthetic inference and drift-estimation experiments, runtime measurements, and analysis of mouse calcium-imaging data.

after.justification: The original empirical studies are retained, with additional Lorenz-attractor experiments in Section 5.1 and Appendices L.1.3 and L.2.

M1.justification: The natural-gradient updates, Gaussian variational family, associative scans, and SING-GP are retained. Monte Carlo was already an expectation-computation option in v1 and is newly evaluated. Although v2 Eq. (9) loses the prior's tilde, the derivations retain the same discretized-prior objective.

E1.justification: V2 adds Lorenz-attractor data for known-drift state inference and joint inference/drift learning. This includes Lorenz dynamics embedded in larger latent spaces with 100-dimensional observations. The linear, place-cell, Duffing, and mouse datasets are retained.

E2.justification: Appendix L.2 newly evaluates SDE Matching against SING; v1 only cited it. This substantially broadens comparison to an amortized neural-SDE variational-posterior method. The existing experiment-specific Kalman smoothing, VDP, Adam, and CMGS comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The new Lorenz studies introduce single-sample Monte Carlo versus six-node-per-dimension quadrature, dimensions 3–50, and specified optimization schedules. The SDE Matching comparison varies training trials from 10 to 1,024 and evaluates normalized drift error on 1,024 independent trajectories. These are added protocols; retained experiments' settings are unchanged.

E4.justification: Figure 4 adds an expectation-estimator ablation testing Monte Carlo against quadrature across latent dimensions, including memory feasibility. Figure 7 adds a training-sample sensitivity comparison with SDE Matching. These extend the existing discretization, runtime-scaling, and neural-data analyses.

E5.justification: V2 specifies five Monte Carlo seeds for Figure 4, with standard errors described as negligible and omitted. Figure 7 reports ±2SE over ten random initializations and algorithm seeds. Existing uncertainty reporting is retained; these disclosures do not establish increased repetitions of earlier experiments.

E6.justification: New Figure 4 reports Monte Carlo/quadrature latent RMSE of 0.1419/0.1417 at D=3 and Monte Carlo RMSE of 0.6778 at D=50. Figure 7 reports, at 100 training trials, latent RMSE 0.50/0.67 and normalized dynamics RMSE 0.29/0.19 for SING/SDE Matching. At 1,024 trials, latent RMSE is 0.58/0.57. Original experimental results are retained.

T1.justification: Appendix E adds a conditional maximizer-consistency argument using compactness and uniform convergence, removes the extra differentiability assumption on A(t), and revises the proof using absolute continuity and explicit diffusion-matrix dependence. Appendix B revises the mean-parameter-space definition and relative-interior treatment. The original square-root discretization-error rate remains.

C1.justification: The abstract, four introductory contributions, and concluding summary retain the central claims about natural-gradient inference, temporal parallelization, continuous-time ELBO approximation, and improved drift estimation. Additional experiments and theoretical arguments support these retained contributions without redefining them.

C2.justification: V2 replaces the explicitly untested high-dimensional-scaling limitation with empirical support for Monte Carlo. Appendix L.2 newly qualifies drift-learning effectiveness through initialization sensitivity and SDE Matching's generally better drift recovery, while proposing full-grid updates as an explanation for SING's latent-state sample efficiency. The discussion also adds learnable inducing-point locations as future work.

D1.justification: Appendices L.1.3 and L.2 add reproducibility details for the new studies: simulation grids, noise parameters, learning-rate schedules, network activation, expectation approximations, and use of the authors' SDE Matching implementation without further tuning. Existing experimental recipes and code/data access information are retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds works by Hasan et al., Wang et al., Zeng et al., and Royden/Fitzpatrick, and expands discussion of the previously cited SDE Matching. Positioning relative to Verma et al., GP regression, and parallel inference remains substantially unchanged. SDE Matching's publication update is not a new cited work.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized prose edits, clarifies trial-specific variational posteriors and uniform convergence, reorganizes parts of Appendix B, and inserts Lorenz subsections. Author/header text and bibliography formatting also change. Most prose and the overall section sequence are retained.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redesigned around the generative model, natural-gradient geometry, and natural parameters. New Figures 4 and 7 display the Lorenz results. The conference layout resizes and relocates figures and introduces wrapped displays. Original experimental graphics are reused; Figure 3E's caption corrects MSE to RMSE.

improvement.justification: V1 explicitly leaves high-dimensional inference untested and lacks an evaluated neural-SDE variational-posterior baseline. V2 addresses both gaps with the Lorenz studies, reports important drift-learning weaknesses, and makes the conditions connecting ELBO convergence to maximizer consistency explicit. These additions substantially strengthen empirical support and clarify applicability. The missing tilde in Eq. (9) is a limited notation defect that does not outweigh these gains.
